column1: What is the core Reactive Streams demand protocol that governs how data flows between a Publisher and Subscriber?
column2: A Subscriber calls Subscription.request(n) to signal it can accept at most n items; the Publisher delivers at most n items. No item crosses the wire without explicit demand.

column1: What is the key distinction between a Flux<T> pipeline's assembly and its execution?
column2: A Flux is a lazy description of a sequence (operator graph/DAG) that performs no work until a Subscriber attaches and issues a demand signal—assembly time is separate from eager subscription-time execution.

column1: What ordering guarantee does the Reactive Streams specification enforce on onNext signals, regardless of thread count?
column2: Sequential delivery: onNext signals are delivered strictly in order, never concurrently, no matter how many threads participate in the pipeline.

column1: What is the fundamental invariant that defines Flux as a GitOps reconciliation engine?
column2: Git commits represent immutable checkpoints of desired cluster state, and every cluster resource must eventually converge to reflect the configuration at the current HEAD of its associated Git branch.

column1: What happens when an operator manually edits a Flux-managed resource with kubectl?
column2: Flux's level-triggered reconciliation loop detects the drift on its next cycle and reverts the change, restoring the Git-declared configuration—making configuration drift mechanically impossible.

column1: Why is Flux's reconciliation model described as 'level-triggered' rather than 'edge-triggered'?
column2: It continuously observes both declared Git state and actual cluster state, computing and correcting the delta on every cycle, rather than reacting only once to a single change event.

column1: What distinguishes a Helm chart's release revision history from Kubernetes object revisions tracked in etcd's MVCC log?
column2: Helm maintains its own independent historical revision chain for release state (via its storage driver, e.g., Secrets or ConfigMaps), separate and not directly correlated with etcd's MVCC-tracked object revisions.

column1: What two-phase commit boundary does the HelmRelease controller enforce before materializing Kubernetes resources?
column2: It must resolve chart dependencies and version constraints (chart rendering) before applying the rendered resources to the cluster (cluster application).

column1: Why do embedded ClusterRole/ClusterRoleBinding definitions in Helm charts pose a multi-tenancy security risk?
column2: They can grant cluster-scoped permissions that allow a compromised tenant to pivot into administrative contexts if admission control policies don't enforce strict capability boundaries.

column1: What are the five structured fields in a Flux Kubernetes status condition?
column2: Type, Status (True/False/Unknown), Reason code, human-readable Message, and Last Transition Timestamp.

column1: What does the monotonic observedGeneration field guarantee in Flux status reporting?
column2: It ensures reported status reflects reconciliation against the latest declared spec, by comparing against metadata.generation to detect whether the controller has processed the most recent change.

column1: Which five specialized controllers does Flux decompose its GitOps responsibilities across?
column2: source-controller (fetches artifacts), kustomize-controller (builds/applies Kustomizations), helm-controller (manages Helm releases), notification-controller (dispatches events), and image-reflector/image-automation-controller (scans registries and commits image updates back to Git).
